name: Fat-loss to reveal neck

lead: Lowering body fat reduces the fat around the chin and neck so the neck and jaw look more defined and a fat-based double chin shrinks. A double-chin look can come from excess fat or from jaw structure.

Overall fat loss from diet and activity reduces subcutaneous fat including around the neck, in an order that varies between people. Exercise physiology sources describe fat as mobilized from the whole body rather than from the area exercised, and where it comes off first is strongly influenced by genetics. A bony cause of a soft profile usually needs surgical correction, and no study has tested fat loss specifically for neck definition.

paras: People combine a calorie deficit, protein-rich eating, resistance training and daily activity, and track their progress over several months. Neck and jaw definition tends to show as overall leanness increases.
No specific risks are documented for this practice. General risks of aggressive dieting apply and are covered in other articles.

angle.text: Cutting body fat reduces submental and neck fat, which shows sharper neck and jaw contours and shrinks a double chin where excess fat is the cause. Where fat comes off first is largely genetic, and a double chin from bone structure usually needs surgical correction.

lead: Fat loss to reveal the neck means lowering body fat so that the neck, submental area (under the chin) and jawline look more defined. People use it to sharpen the line between jaw and neck, reduce a soft or 'double chin' look and show more of the underlying bone structure.[1]

Wikipedia notes that a double chin can arise from excess fat around the neck in some overweight people, or from a bony deficiency in people of normal weight, with the fat form responding to weight loss and the bony form usually needing surgical correction.[1] Exercise-physiology sources describe fat as mobilised from the whole body rather than from the area exercised, with genetics strongly influencing where it is lost first.[2]

Face research also supports the general idea that leanness shapes how faces are perceived: a 2009 University of St Andrews study (Coetzee, Perrett and Stephen) found young men rated women of average weight as most attractive and healthy-looking, and that heavier students reported more frequent colds and higher blood pressure.[3] No study has tested fat loss specifically for neck or jawline definition.

paras: The Wikipedia article on double chin describes two causes: excess subcutaneous fat around the neck, and underdeveloped jaw bones that leave the chin blending into the neck. Fat-related cases may be treated by removing the fat pad, sometimes with a hyoid lift, while bone-related cases may need genioplasty or orthognathic surgery.[1] People pursuing fat loss for this goal therefore tend to distinguish the two.

The Wikipedia article on spot reduction states that physiologists and fitness bodies regard it as disproven and that fat loss follows overall diet and exercise, with genetics shaping where it is lost. It cites a 2011 study of 24 sedentary adults who did abdominal exercises for six weeks and showed no decrease in abdominal subcutaneous fat.[2] That study concerned the abdomen, not the neck.

The St Andrews study found that perceived facial weight was linked to ratings of attractiveness and health, with average-weight faces rated highest by young male raters.[3] This is the research base people point to when treating leanness as a face-improving step.
No studies found on fat loss for neck or jawline appearance. Related research on abdominal exercise and regional fat,[2] and on perceived facial weight,[3] is summarised above.
